prerequisites.meaning: An integer identifying a text unit in one particular tokenizer's vocabulary.
prerequisites.check: Must two different tokenizers assign the same IDs to 'Dublin'?
prerequisites.answer: No. Each tokenizer has its own vocabulary and its own IDs.

prerequisites.meaning: Nonnegative probabilities for possible outcomes, adding to one.
prerequisites.answer: Yes. All values are non-negative and 0.6 + 0.3 + 0.1 = 1.

prerequisites.meaning: A model predicting the next token from the tokens already present.
prerequisites.check: What input is available before the next answer token is generated?
prerequisites.answer: Only the prompt and any tokens already generated, never later tokens.

diagrams.title: A decoder chat request
diagrams.subtitle: Trace a user's question through the local model
trace: The question 'What is the capital of Ireland?' is placed in a user message.
The chat template adds the role and assistant-start formatting expected by Qwen.
Generation repeatedly predicts another token until stopping or reaching its budget.
The code slices off the input so the returned answer contains new tokens only.
The same helper returns a token count and elapsed seconds for comparison.
diagrams.explanation: A chat interface hides several transformations. First, the user's question becomes a message with a role. A chat template adds the model-specific formatting that distinguishes user text from the assistant reply. The tokenizer converts that formatted input into IDs. The decoder then predicts successive tokens; its generation settings determine how each prediction is chosen. The returned tensor includes both the input and generated continuation, so the helper slices away the input before decoding the answer. No training happens during this call: the model's learned weights stay fixed. The lab compares this decoder workflow with BERT's masked-token prediction and Flan-T5's separate input encoder and output decoder. Those families perform different operations even when their demonstrations use similar questions. The token count and elapsed time describe this measured call, rather than guaranteeing answer quality.
diagrams.check_question: Why does chat slice the generated tensor at the original input length?
diagrams.check_answer: Because decoder generation returns input IDs followed by the continuation; the helper returns only the new answer.

diagrams.title: Choose one next token
diagrams.subtitle: Separate model scores from the decoding policy
diagrams.feedback: Repeat from the extended prefix; model weights stay fixed.
trace: The lab's five scores [2, 1, 0.5, 0.1, −1] give probabilities about [0.56, 0.21, 0.12, 0.08, 0.03].
Top-k with k=2 retains the two highest-scoring candidates in this example.
Top-p with p=0.8 instead retains three: their cumulative probability first exceeds 0.8.
Removed candidates get zero probability; retained probabilities are renormalised.
Sampling selects one ID, which is appended before the next model call.
diagrams.explanation: The neural model provides logits, unnormalised scores for all vocabulary tokens. Decoding is the policy used to turn those scores into a continuation. Greedy decoding chooses the highest-scoring token; the sample helper instead draws a token from probabilities. Temperature rescales logits: a lower positive value concentrates probability on stronger candidates, while a higher value spreads it. Top-k filtering uses a score threshold based on the kth candidate; ties at that threshold can retain additional tokens. Top-p filtering keeps enough leading candidates to reach a chosen cumulative probability, so its retained count depends on model confidence. The chosen token changes the next prefix and therefore the next prediction. A more diverse output is not necessarily more accurate. The manual loop runs its specified number of steps; it does not contain an explicit end-of-sequence stopping test.
diagrams.check_question: Why can top-p retain different numbers of candidates at successive positions?
diagrams.check_answer: The probability distribution changes with the prefix; a confident distribution needs fewer candidates to reach p.

diagrams.title: Compare models with evidence
diagrams.subtitle: Different experiments answer different comparison questions

steps.title: Change decoding
steps.detail: Hold the prefix and model fixed

trace: Count tokens for identical source text before comparing the models' outputs.
BERT fills [MASK]; T5 and Qwen generate text using different architectures.
Use the same story prefix for greedy, beam and sampled continuations.
Treat perplexity under different tokenisers as different prediction measurements.
For the scheduling puzzle, compare final-answer correctness, tokens and time across runs.
diagrams.explanation: This lab is a sequence of comparison experiments, rather than one shared model pipeline. Token counts show how the same text becomes different pieces. The family demonstrations then expose different output interfaces: BERT ranks words for a blank, Flan-T5 transforms input text into output text, and Qwen continues a formatted conversation. Decoding experiments keep a story prefix fixed while changing how tokens are selected. Perplexity measures the predictability of supplied text, but differences in token boundaries prevent a direct per-token ranking across model families. The call log measures output length and elapsed time. Finally, the thinking experiment checks final numerical answers across sampled seeds, rather than trusting persuasive intermediate text. Different mode settings also use different token budgets and sampling parameters, so the comparison reflects the complete settings used, rather than isolating the thinking switch alone.
diagrams.check_question: Can lower perplexity from one tokenizer prove that its model answers questions better?
diagrams.check_answer: No. Tokenisers define different prediction units, and text predictability is not the same measurement as question-answer correctness.

diagrams.title: How pre-training learns a language model
diagrams.insert_before_title: The LLM pipeline, in more detail
diagrams.subtitle: This is the developer's training process. This week's lab uses already trained models.
diagrams.explanation: Pre-training learns general language patterns from text. The text supplies both input tokens and known next-token targets. A decoder with a causal mask predicts scores without reading future answers. Cross-entropy measures prediction error, and the optimiser adjusts the learned weights. Developers repeat this across many batches and check held-out text. Post-training then uses instruction examples and feedback to improve assistant behaviour. This is a conceptual process diagram, not a claim that the week 6 lab pre-trains an LLM. The lab loads published weights and compares inference behaviour. The target branch goes directly to the loss. The dashed loop belongs to the weight-update step; post-training happens after pre-training.
trace: For a token sequence [A, B, C, D], inputs [A, B, C] pair with targets [B, C, D].
The first position predicts B using A. The second predicts C using A and B.
The training update changes weights. A later chat request uses those learned weights.
Two assistants can differ because of pre-training, post-training or the application around the model.
diagrams.check_question: Does the week 6 pipeline call learn new weights from your question?
diagrams.check_answer: No. It loads pretrained weights and runs inference. The diagram describes how developers trained those weights earlier.
diagrams.feedback: Repeat pre-training batches; the optimiser changes model weights.

diagrams.title: Read a local or hosted chat call end to end
diagrams.insert_before_title: Querying a hosted model through an API
diagrams.subtitle: A request contains messages and settings. The result includes text and usage evidence.
diagrams.explanation: A local request applies the chat template and creates input IDs before generation. A hosted API accepts role/content messages and lets its provider format and run the model. These are alternative routes; the client does not normally send its locally tokenised IDs to a chat API. Local decoder outputs include the input prefix, which must be sliced away. Hosted chat responses already separate the answer message. Record model, settings, date, usage and time, then check correctness. Keep keys in secrets; availability and usage fields depend on the provider.
trace: Send a user message asking for one sentence explaining tokens.
Set max_new_tokens to a small answer budget for the local call.
Compare the returned answer with the request. The original question should not appear as generated output.
Log local timing or hosted usage and keep the same prompt when comparing models.
diagrams.check_question: Why can token counts differ for the same question sent to two models?
diagrams.check_answer: The models may use different tokenizers and chat templates. Compare each model's actual formatted input and output counts.

glossary.meaning: A network producing contextual representations of an input sequence.
A network predicting output tokens using the preceding output tokens and available input context.
Model-specific formatting used to represent roles and messages as a token sequence.
A positive divisor on logits that changes the concentration of sampling probabilities.
The leading token candidates retained by a top-p cumulative-probability threshold.
The elapsed time taken to produce a response.

pitfalls: A fluent answer can still be wrong; output diversity is a different measure from correctness.
Few examples inside a prompt change context, rather than updating the model's weights.
Visible thinking text and a longer token budget do not guarantee a correct final answer.

recap.question: Does a longer thinking trace prove a better answer?
recap.answer: No. Check final correctness, whether it finished, tokens and time on realistic examples.
recap.next: In Week 7 we write prompts and measure whether changes help.
recap.notes: Say: Place today’s ideas along one request. Training created the weights earlier. The current message is formatted and tokenised, fits a context budget, and produces scores. Decoding chooses an output; checking establishes whether it met the task. Analogy: a tool’s design, availability and settings are separate entries on its datasheet. Ask students to contrast BERT mask filling, T5 text-to-text and a decoder continuation. Common mistake: an open-weight release is not automatically unrestricted or fully open source. Read the model card and exact licence, then evaluate accuracy, latency, token cost and failure cases. Extra thinking must earn its extra computation.
